The Mindanao glassgoby Gobiopterus mindanensis is a diminutive gobiid, the adults of which typically attain an ultimate total length of only 1.6 centimeters [Li = 1.6 centimeters]. This strikingly small body size places it among the smallest known vertebrate species and constrains nearly every aspect of its life history. Early development is brief; at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C], embryos complete incubation and the yolk-sac larvae emerge from the chorion after approximately five days [ab = approximately five days]. The newly hatched prolarvae are minute, weighing just 0.000212 grams [Wwb = 0.000212 grams] at the moment of eclosion, a figure that underscores the extreme energetic constraints operating at this lower limit of vertebrate body mass.

Sexual maturation in this species occurs at a surprisingly small size. Histological examination of the gonads indicates that puberty is attained when individuals reach a total length of roughly 0.7 centimeters [Lp = roughly 0.7 centimeters]. At this ontogenetic milestone, the corresponding somatic mass is similarly modest; a fish at the point of reproductive activation weighs approximately 0.0033 grams [Wwp = approximately 0.0033 grams]. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) in reproductively active females has been measured at 28.5% [GSI = 28.5%] at a water temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. These reproductive measurements were all gathered from specimens maintained at the stable thermal regime of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] characteristic of their shallow freshwater habitats.

The adult body size trajectory of Gobiopterus mindanensis is tightly constrained. Asymptotic growth plateaus at an ultimate wet weight of just 0.04 grams [Wwi = 0.04 grams], a value that represents the maximum body mass attained by fully mature individuals. The contrast between this adult mass and the much smaller juvenile form is considerable: a fish at the initiation of its reproductive life weighs only 0.0033 grams [Wwp = 0.0033 grams], meaning that body mass more than doubles during the final phases of somatic growth preceding the onset of breeding. This pattern suggests that early reproduction is traded off against continued investment in somatic expansion, a classic life-history trade-off common among small-bodied teleosts.

Lifespan data for this species were derived from a mark-recapture study conducted under the controlled thermal conditions of a laboratory mesocosm maintained at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The maximum recorded lifespan was 120 days [am = 120 days], a remarkably short duration that situates Gobiopterus mindanensis among the most rapidly lived vertebrates at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. Within this compressed lifetime, the brief embryonic period of only about five days [ab = about five days] at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C] allows for extremely rapid generational turnover. Females become reproductively active soon after reaching the length-at-puberty of 0.7 centimeters [Lp = 0.7 centimeters], and the gonadosomatic index was 28.5% [GSI = 28.5%] at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C].

Density-dependent effects on growth are likely pronounced in this species given its small adult size. In crowded conditions, competition for food resources probably delays the attainment of the ultimate total length of 1.6 centimeters [Li = 1.6 centimeters] and may reduce the ultimate wet weight below the asymptotic value of 0.04 grams [Wwi = 0.04 grams]. Conversely, under optimal conditions with abundant microinvertebrate prey, individuals might approach the theoretical maximum lifespan of 120 days [am = 120 days] more regularly at a temperature of 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C]. The overall life-history strategy of Gobiopterus mindanensis thus conforms to a pattern of extreme miniaturization, rapid development, short lifespan, and high reproductive allocation, all orchestrated within the narrow thermal envelope of its freshwater habitat at 27.3 °C [T = 27.3 °C].
